items.title: [Real Estate 101 #2] Two Identical Houses, One $60,000 Gap: Why Land Breaks the Rules of Ordinary Goods
items.body:
> Real estate behaves unlike almost any other asset because it can't move, can't be duplicated, and can't be manufactured on demand — and everything from your property tax bill to your listing price traces back to those few stubborn facts.

## Today's Concept

Most goods you buy are interchangeable. A gallon of milk in Boise is the same gallon of milk in Miami. If demand jumps, factories make more. If it breaks, you replace it.

Land does none of that. Real estate scholars sort its oddities into two buckets.

**Natural characteristics** — the ones physics and geography impose, which no law or contract can undo:

- **Immobility.** A parcel cannot be relocated. You can move the lumber; you cannot move the lot. This is why real estate markets are stubbornly *local*: a glut of condos in Miami does nothing for a shortage in Denver.
- **Fixed supply.** The amount of land at a given location is essentially set. Landfill and reclamation add a rounding error at the margins, but no one is manufacturing new blocks in downtown Chicago. When demand rises, price does the adjusting, because quantity mostly can't.
- **Indestructibility.** Land isn't consumed by use. The *building* on it wears out — that's why the IRS lets you depreciate a residential structure over 27.5 years but **never** lets you depreciate the land underneath it.
- **Heterogeneity.** No two parcels occupy the same point on Earth, so no two are truly identical. Even side-by-side lots differ in slope, sun, corner exposure, and traffic noise.
- **Adjacency.** Every parcel is stuck next to its neighbors and absorbs their effects — a good school on one side, a rendering plant on the other.

**Human (economic and institutional) characteristics** — the ones people create, and therefore can change:

- **Flexibility of use.** The same dirt can be a parking lot, a duplex, or a data center, depending on zoning and economics. Appraisers formalize this as **highest and best use**.
- **Divisibility and assembly.** One parcel can be subdivided into ten; ten can be assembled into one. Developers profit precisely from this — a "site assembly" of five small lots is often worth more than the five sold separately.
- **Variable position.** Physical location never moves, but *economic* location moves constantly. A new interchange, a rezoning, a light-rail stop, or a school-district boundary redraw can reprice a parcel that has not changed by a single inch.

Then there's **classification by use** — the shorthand the industry actually trades on: **residential** (1–4 units), **commercial** (office, retail, multifamily of 5+ units, hotels), **industrial** (warehouse, manufacturing, logistics), **land** (raw, agricultural, entitled lots), and **special purpose** (churches, schools, self-storage, marinas). These labels aren't cosmetic. They determine which zoning code applies, which loan product you qualify for, how the property is appraised, and who your buyer pool is.

## In Everyday Life

Picture a builder in a Charlotte, North Carolina suburb who puts up forty homes from the same three floor plans. Same trusses, same countertops, same paint. On paper, units 12 and 31 are clones.

Unit 12 sits on a cul-de-sac backing onto a greenway. Unit 31 backs onto a six-lane arterial. Five years later, unit 12 sells for around $60,000 more. Nothing about the *house* explains the gap — that's **heterogeneity** and **adjacency** doing the work. You could not fix it by swapping the houses, because you can't swap the lots: **immobility**.

Now the county approves a new highway interchange half a mile north and rezones the frontage from single-family to neighborhood commercial. A parcel that had been worth roughly $180,000 as a home site gets an offer from a grocery developer at several times that. The parcel is identical to what it was the week before. What changed was its **economic position** and its permitted **use** — a human characteristic, written by a planning board rather than by geology.

And the grocery developer doesn't want one lot. They quietly option four adjacent parcels to build a five-acre pad — **assembly**, where the whole is worth more than the parts. Meanwhile the homeowner across the street discovers her property tax assessment jumped, because the assessor now sees a different neighborhood.

Every step of that story is one of the characteristics above, playing out in dollars.

## Three-Line Summary

1. **Natural characteristics** — immobility, fixed supply, indestructibility, heterogeneity, adjacency — make real estate a local, non-substitutable, supply-inelastic asset, and no contract can override them.
2. **Human characteristics** — use flexibility, divisibility and assembly, variable economic position — are the ones people *can* change, which is exactly where development profit and policy risk live.
3. **Classification by use** (residential, commercial, industrial, land, special purpose) determines the zoning, the financing, the appraisal method, and the buyer pool — so it's a practical category, not an academic one.

## ✅ Self-Quiz

**1. Which of the following is a *natural* characteristic of real estate?**
A. Zoning designation
B. Immobility
C. Highest and best use
D. The ability to subdivide a parcel

**2. True or False (O/X):** Because land is indestructible, U.S. tax rules let owners depreciate both the land and the building on it.

**3. A city rezones a residential parcel to allow a retail strip center, and its market value triples. Which characteristic best explains this?**
A. Indestructibility
B. Adjacency
C. Variability of economic position and use
D. Fixed supply

## 📚 Today's Terms

- **Immobility** — The physical fact that a parcel cannot be moved, which forces real estate markets to be local rather than national.
- **Heterogeneity (non-homogeneity)** — The principle that no two parcels are identical, which is why appraisers adjust comparable sales instead of quoting a single market price.
- **Inelastic supply** — Supply that barely responds to price, so demand shocks in real estate show up mostly as price movement rather than new quantity.
- **Highest and best use** — The legally permitted, physically possible, financially feasible use that produces the greatest value for a site; the starting point of most appraisals.
- **Entitlement** — The package of government approvals (zoning, permits, plat approval) that unlocks a specific use for a parcel; often the single largest driver of land value.
- **Site assembly** — Combining adjacent parcels under one owner to create a larger, more valuable development site.

---

*Answers: **1 — B.** Immobility is imposed by geography; zoning, highest and best use, and subdivision are all human-made and therefore changeable. **2 — False (X).** Land is not depreciable precisely because it isn't consumed; only the improvement is (27.5 years for residential rental, 39 for most commercial, under current U.S. rules — check with a tax professional for your situation). **3 — C.** The parcel did not move and did not change physically; its permitted use and economic position changed, which is the classic human characteristic at work.*

items.title: [ICRA 2025] A Prosthetic Hand With One Motor, 19 Joints, and a Direct Line to Your Nerves
items.body:
> At robotics' biggest conference, TUM's Cristina Piazza argued that the next generation of artificial limbs won't come from bigger computers alone — it will come from hands whose *bodies* are smart enough to do half the work, paired with control signals read closer to the nervous system.

## What Was Presented

On Tuesday, May 20, 2025, at IEEE ICRA in Atlanta — the largest annual gathering in robotics — **Cristina Piazza** of the Technical University of Munich delivered a keynote titled *"Towards Bioinspired Bionic Limbs: From Embodied Intelligence to Neural Control."* Piazza leads TUM's Professorship of Healthcare and Rehabilitation Robotics; she earned her PhD in robotics at the University of Pisa and did postdoctoral work at Northwestern University and the Shirley Ryan AbilityLab's Center for Bionic Medicine in Chicago.

*A note on sourcing: ICRA did not publish a written abstract for this keynote, only the title, session details, and a recording. What follows describes the research program the title refers to, drawn from Piazza's published work — not a transcript of the talk.*

The talk's two halves map onto two long-standing problems in prosthetics.

**The body half — "embodied intelligence."** A human hand has more than twenty joints. The obvious engineering answer is a motor per joint, which gives you a heavy, fragile, expensive hand that a user must consciously drive joint by joint. The alternative Piazza has worked on for a decade is to build the intelligence into the mechanics instead. The Pisa/IIT SoftHand — whose foundational 2014 paper lists Piazza among its authors — has **19 joints driven by a single motor**, linked by an elastic tendon running through all of them. Pull the tendon and the hand closes; when a finger meets an object, it stops, and the remaining slack redistributes to the fingers still free to move. The hand wraps around a mug, a doorknob, or an egg without anyone computing the grasp. The design borrows a neuroscience idea called **synergies**: the observation that human hand postures cluster along a small number of coordinated patterns rather than exploring all their degrees of freedom independently.

**The control half — "neural control."** Conventional powered prostheses read muscle activity from skin electrodes (surface EMG) on the residual limb: flex to close, extend to open. It works, but it's coarse, drifts as the user sweats or shifts the socket, and forces people to learn an unnatural mapping. Piazza's group has published on simultaneous myoelectric control for multi-degree-of-freedom below-elbow prostheses, on multi-synergistic soft bionic hands tested with people who have limb loss, and more recently on **high-density surface EMG** — dense electrode grids that capture far richer signals than a couple of contacts. The direction across this field is to decode the activity of individual **motoneurons** — the spinal cells that actually command muscle fibers — rather than the blurred muscle signal that sits on top of them. A January 2025 *Science Robotics* paper from collaborating groups at IIT and Imperial College London (Capsi-Morales, Barsakcioglu, Catalano, Grioli, Bicchi, and Farina) reported that this neural-synergy approach let prosthesis users hit target hand postures 82.5% of the time, versus 35.0% with conventional muscle-synergy control.

Piazza's own work has also been road-tested in public: she led the SoftHand Pro team to **second place in the Cybathlon 2020 Global Edition** powered arm prosthesis race, a competition where people with disabilities perform everyday tasks — opening jars, handling cutlery, hanging laundry — under a clock.

## Why It Matters

Prosthetic abandonment is the field's quiet scandal. A meaningful share of people fitted with advanced powered arms stop using them, often because the device is heavy, tiring to control, or slower than just adapting. A hand with many motors and many buttons can look impressive in a lab video and still lose to a simple hook in a kitchen.

The embodied-intelligence argument attacks this from the hardware side: if the mechanism absorbs the complexity, the device gets lighter, cheaper, more robust to being banged against a table, and — critically — needs far less from the user's attention. The neural-control argument attacks it from the human side: if the signal comes from something closer to the original motor command, the limb starts to feel less like a tool being operated and more like a part of the body.

Neither half is sufficient alone. A brilliant neural decoder driving a rigid twenty-motor hand still demands constant supervision. A beautifully compliant hand driven by two crude electrodes still can't express what the user intends. The keynote's framing — *from* embodied intelligence *to* neural control — is a claim that the two have to be designed together, with the hardware and the interface meeting in the middle.

The same principles spill outward: the underactuated, compliant designs that make good prosthetic hands also make good robot grippers for warehouses and good actuators for rehabilitation exoskeletons and assistive robots that touch people.

## An Easy Way to Think About It

Think about picking up a paper coffee cup in the dark.

You don't measure the cup, plan five finger trajectories, and execute them. You just close your hand. Your fingers land where the cup is, the soft pads deform around it, and the grip settles — your *hand* solved most of the problem before your brain got involved. That's embodied intelligence: intelligence stored in shape, softness, and mechanical coupling rather than in computation.

Now imagine giving someone driving directions. Shouting "left! left! now right!" through a closed window is surface EMG — the message gets through, distorted and late. Sitting in the passenger seat and pointing is high-density, motoneuron-level decoding: the same intent, delivered with far more of the original detail intact. Piazza's argument is that you want both — a car that handles well *and* a passenger who can actually be heard.

## Three-Line Recap

1. Piazza's ICRA 2025 keynote linked two threads of bionic limb research: mechanically "smart" soft hands, like the 19-joint, single-motor Pisa/IIT SoftHand, and control signals read closer to the nervous system.
2. Building intelligence into the mechanism makes limbs lighter, tougher, and cheaper while cutting the mental effort of using them; better neural decoding makes them feel like part of the body rather than a machine being operated.
3. The point is the pairing — hardware and neural interface designed as one system, validated on real users in clinics and at events like the Cybathlon, not just in the lab.

## 📚 Today's Terms

- **Embodied intelligence** — Useful behavior that comes from a robot's physical structure (softness, elasticity, mechanical coupling) rather than from its software.
- **Synergy** — In motor neuroscience, a coordinated pattern of joint or muscle activity; a small set of synergies explains most everyday hand postures, so copying them lets a few actuators cover many grasps.
- **Underactuation** — Having fewer motors than moving joints, letting mechanical coupling and contact with an object decide the rest of the shape.
- **Myoelectric control (sEMG)** — Driving a prosthesis from electrical activity picked up by electrodes on the skin over residual muscles; high-density sEMG uses a dense grid of contacts for a much richer signal.
- **Motoneuron** — The spinal nerve cell that sends the final command to muscle fibers; decoding motoneuron activity gets closer to the user's original intent than reading the muscle signal alone.

---

**Sources:** [ICRA 2025 keynote sessions](https://2025.ieee-icra.org/program/keynote-sessions/) · [talk recording](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XLnszZk4Y6c) · [Piazza's TUM lab page](https://www.ce.cit.tum.de/en/nhcr/members/cpiazza/) · [Adaptive synergies for the Pisa/IIT SoftHand (IJRR 2014)](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/0278364913518998) · [The SoftHand Pro platform (J NeuroEng Rehabil 2023)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12984-023-01130-x) · [Merging motoneuron and postural synergies (Science Robotics 2025)](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/scirobotics.ado9509)

items.title: A Toll Booth on the World's Oil Highway: Inside the Iran–Oman Plan to Reopen Hormuz
items.body:
The proposal now circulating among Gulf capitals is deceptively simple. Tankers heading into the Persian Gulf would use one designated inbound lane, monitored on the Iranian side. Tankers heading out would use a separate lane on the Omani side. Ships would clear a joint notification system before entering, and they would pay what the framework reportedly calls a "service fee" — money described as covering escort, traffic management, spill response and environmental monitoring.

Regional officials cited in recent reporting say the arrangement is close to final. If it holds, it would end the most disruptive interruption to global energy shipping in decades. It would also hand Tehran something it did not have before the fighting began: a formal, revenue-generating role in managing traffic through the single most important chokepoint in the world economy.

That is the tension at the center of this story, and it is why the plan has run into a wall in Washington. President Donald Trump has said publicly that the United States will not accept Iran charging ships to pass. The framework's supporters say the fee is a technical cost-recovery measure. Its critics say a toll is a toll, and that once it exists, it never goes away.

**A note on sourcing:** the details below reflect what officials and analysts have described publicly. No final text has been released, and the terms could change or collapse entirely. Readers should treat specifics as provisional.

---

## Why this particular stretch of water matters so much

The Strait of Hormuz is roughly 21 nautical miles across at its narrowest point — about the distance from Manhattan to the middle of Long Island. The usable shipping channels are far narrower: two lanes of about two miles each, separated by a two-mile buffer, threading between Iranian waters to the north and Omani territory to the south.

Through that gap moves something on the order of a fifth of the world's traded oil, along with a comparable share of seaborne liquefied natural gas, most of it from Qatar. Saudi Arabia, Iraq, the UAE, Kuwait and Iran itself all ship the bulk of their crude through it. There are pipeline workarounds — Saudi Arabia's East-West line to the Red Sea and the UAE's line to Fujairah — but together they can carry only a fraction of normal Hormuz volumes.

There is no substitute route. That single fact is what makes the strait valuable, and what makes any change to who manages it a matter of global consequence rather than regional housekeeping.

## How the two-lane system would work

Under the framework as described, the arrangement rests on three pillars.

**Split sovereignty over traffic.** Inbound vessels would transit a corridor supervised from the Iranian side; outbound vessels would use an Omani-supervised corridor. Both countries would contribute to a joint coordination cell handling vessel notifications, scheduling and incident response.

**A notification-and-clearance step.** Ships would file details in advance — flag, cargo, ownership, destination. Supporters present this as standard maritime traffic management, similar in spirit to systems used in other busy waterways. Skeptics note that a clearance step is also a screening step, and screening is leverage.

**The fee.** Vessels would pay a per-transit charge, framed as compensation for security escort, navigational services and environmental protection. Reported figures have varied widely and none should be treated as settled.

Oman's participation is the element that makes the package politically viable. Muscat has spent decades as the region's quiet intermediary — on good terms with Tehran, Washington, Riyadh and others simultaneously. Its presence lets shipowners and insurers describe the arrangement as multilateral rather than as an Iranian tollgate, and it gives Gulf states a counterpart they are willing to deal with.

## The money is smaller than it sounds — and bigger

Run the arithmetic and the direct cost looks modest. A very large crude carrier holds roughly two million barrels. A fee in the low hundreds of thousands of dollars spreads out to a few cents per barrel — noise against a crude price in the dollars-per-barrel swing range on any given week. Charterers absorb worse every month from bunker fuel moves.

But the fee is not really where the cost lives. The cost lives in insurance.

War-risk premiums for Gulf transits reprice constantly against perceived threat, and during acute periods they have jumped by multiples, sometimes adding far more per voyage than any proposed service fee. If the framework genuinely stabilizes transits — if underwriters believe escorted, deconflicted passage means fewer incidents — premiums fall, and shipowners could come out ahead even after paying. That is the commercial argument its backers make, and it is not a weak one.

The counterargument is about precedent rather than price. A fee that is small today is still a fee, and a mechanism that exists can be adjusted. Tie the rate to a vessel's flag, owner or destination, and a traffic-management system becomes an instrument of policy. Nothing in the reported framework suggests that is the intent. Nothing in it would obviously prevent it either.

## The legal argument nobody fully wins

International law treats natural straits differently from canals, and that distinction explains most of the dispute.

The Suez and Panama canals are engineered waterways, built and maintained by states that legitimately charge for their use. Hormuz is a natural channel. Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, ships enjoy a right of transit passage through straits used for international navigation, and the convention bars states bordering a strait from levying charges on foreign vessels solely for passing through. Fees for specific services actually rendered — pilotage, salvage, traffic control — sit in a narrower and more defensible category.

The complication is that the parties do not stand on identical ground. Iran signed UNCLOS but never ratified it and has long maintained positions on transit rights that differ from the American reading. The United States never ratified the convention either, yet treats its navigation provisions as binding customary law and has enforced that view with naval presence for decades.

So both sides can cite the law and mean different things. There is also a partial precedent working in Tehran's favor: under the Montreux Convention, Turkey levies cost-recovery charges on ships transiting its straits for services such as lighthouses and health inspection. The amounts are small and the legal basis is specific, but the principle — a strait state charging for services — is established.

Expect the final text, if there is one, to be drafted with enormous care around a single word: whether the payment is for *passage* or for *services*.

## What each side gets

For Iran, the appeal is straightforward. A recognized administrative role converts pressure into position, generates revenue outside sanctioned oil channels, and creates a standing arrangement that would be politically awkward to unwind later.

For Gulf exporters, reopening restores the revenue their budgets depend on. Extended disruption is not a tolerable equilibrium for any producer in the region, including Iran.

For shipowners and cargo owners, predictability is the product. Commercial shipping does not need a favorable outcome so much as a legible one — a known rule, a known cost, a known route.

For Washington, the calculus is harder. Ending the disruption is a clear win. Accepting a permanent Iranian hand on the throttle of global energy trade is a clear loss. The administration's position appears to be that it can have the first without the second, which is why the fee — the smallest number in the package — has become the largest obstacle.

## What to watch

- **The wording.** "Service charge" versus "transit fee" is not semantics. It determines whether the arrangement can be described as consistent with existing law.
- **Who collects.** A jointly administered fund with published accounts reads very differently from direct payment to a national authority.
- **Whether it is flag-blind.** A uniform charge applied to all vessels is a traffic system. A differentiated one is leverage.
- **Duration and review.** A defined sunset with renewal conditions is a temporary fix. An open-ended arrangement is a new permanent feature of the map.
- **Insurance rates.** The most honest indicator of whether markets believe any of this will be what underwriters do with war-risk premiums, not what officials say at podiums.

## The bottom line

The choice on the table is between two imperfect outcomes: a closed or unreliable strait that damages nearly everyone, or an open strait on terms that leave Tehran with more standing than it held before. Neither is anyone's preferred result, and the negotiation is essentially about which imperfection is easier to live with.

The plan's real test is not whether it reopens the waterway. It is whether the mechanism that reopens it can be retired later — or whether the toll booth, once built, simply becomes part of the road.

---

*This article is an analytical explainer based on publicly reported information available at the time of writing. Terms described here are unconfirmed and subject to change. It is not investment, legal, or operational advice.*

items.title: Should Judges Campaign? Kansas Just Voted on the Last Bar-Controlled Court in America
items.body:
On Tuesday, August 4, Kansas voters weighed in on a question most states settled generations ago: who should get to pick the people who decide what the state constitution means?

The measure on the ballot — Amendment 1 — would abolish the Kansas Supreme Court Nominating Commission, the body that has screened candidates for the state's highest court since 1958, and replace the entire appointment process with direct statewide elections. It is a structural change, not a policy one. But almost nobody in Kansas has been arguing about it in structural terms.

Here is what was actually on the ballot, how Kansas ended up as an outlier, and why a fight over judicial paperwork became one of the most heavily contested items on an August primary ballot.

---

## What the amendment would actually do

The proposal is short, and its mechanics matter more than the slogans on either side.

- **It eliminates the nominating commission.** The nine-member body that currently vets applicants and forwards names to the governor would cease to exist.
- **It replaces appointment with election.** All seven justices would be chosen by Kansas voters statewide.
- **Terms stay at six years**, but the ballot cycle is staggered: positions 1, 2 and 3 would be elected in November 2028; positions 4 and 5 in 2030; positions 6 and 7 in 2032; and every six years after that.
- **The Legislature decides the format.** The amendment itself does not specify whether judicial races would be partisan (with party labels on the ballot) or nonpartisan. That call would be left to lawmakers in a future session — a detail that became a significant point of contention during the campaign.
- **Restrictions on judicial political activity would be repealed.** Provisions in Article 3 of the Kansas Constitution limiting justices' party involvement and campaign fundraising would come off the books, since a candidate for office needs to be able to campaign.

Nothing would change immediately. Even under approval, the first election under the new system would not occur until November 2028, and sitting justices would hold their seats until the scheduled election for their position.

---

## The system Kansas has now

Under the current process, a vacancy on the Kansas Supreme Court triggers a three-step sequence.

First, the Supreme Court Nominating Commission reviews applicants and selects three finalists. Second, the governor must appoint one of those three — the governor cannot go outside the list, and if the governor does not act within the constitutional window, the appointment authority passes to the chief justice. There is no confirmation vote by the Kansas Senate. Third, the new justice faces a yes-or-no retention election at the next general election after serving at least a year, and again every six years.

The commission itself is where Kansas stands alone. It has nine members: **five attorneys elected by members of the Kansas bar** — one from each congressional district plus a chairperson elected statewide by lawyers — and **four non-attorneys appointed by the governor**.

That five-to-four split is the whole controversy in one line. Roughly 21 states use some form of nominating commission. Kansas is the only one in which the state bar selects a majority of the commissioners, meaning the licensed legal profession, rather than any elected official, holds the deciding votes on who reaches the shortlist.

---

## How Kansas got here

The 1958 design was itself a reform, and a reaction to a specific scandal.

In the mid-1950s, Governor Fred Hall lost his party's primary. Shortly before his term ended, a vacancy opened on the Supreme Court. Hall resigned, his lieutenant governor was sworn in as governor, and the new governor promptly appointed Hall to the court. Kansas newspapers called it the "Triple Play," and the backlash was immediate. Two years later, voters approved the commission system specifically to take raw appointment power away from a governor acting alone.

That history is why both sides in 2026 could claim to be the reformers. Supporters of the amendment argue the 1958 fix created a different concentration of power — one held by an unelected professional guild. Opponents argue the fix worked exactly as designed and that dismantling it invites the problem it was built to prevent.

Nationally, Kansas would not be doing anything exotic by switching. Roughly 21 states already elect their supreme court justices — about 13 through nonpartisan races and eight through partisan ones. Kansas would become the 22nd.

---

## Why the vote happened now

The proximate trigger was a line of rulings, and one in particular.

In 2019, the Kansas Supreme Court held that Section 1 of the Kansas Constitution's Bill of Rights protects a right to personal autonomy that includes decisions about abortion — a ruling that made the state constitution, not the Legislature, the controlling document on the issue. In August 2022, voters rejected a proposed amendment that would have reversed that interpretation, by roughly 59% to 41% in a primary election that drew unusually heavy turnout. That November, all six justices on the retention ballot were retained, with support ranging from about 65% to 73%.

After 2022, Attorney General Kris Kobach publicly urged legislators to put judicial selection itself before voters. In 2025, they did. Senate Concurrent Resolution 1611 cleared the Kansas Senate 27–13 and the House 84–40 — in both chambers, exactly the two-thirds minimum required to refer a constitutional amendment. Every yes vote came from a Republican. Counting both chambers, about 93% of Republicans who voted supported it; no Democrat did.

Lawmakers also chose to place the question on the August primary ballot rather than the November general election. Supporters argued the measure deserved its own spotlight and pointed to 2022 as proof that Kansans turn out for constitutional questions. Critics argued August primaries usually draw a smaller and less representative electorate.

---

## The argument, taken seriously on both sides

Strip away the campaign advertising and there are two coherent positions.

**The case for elections.** Judicial decisions are, unavoidably, exercises in judgment about contested values. If a court is going to make consequential calls on constitutional meaning, the people affected should have direct say over who sits there. The current design gives a self-selecting professional group — several thousand licensed attorneys — a structural majority over a shortlist the governor cannot depart from. That is real public power with no electoral check attached. Retention elections, supporters note, almost never remove anyone; no Kansas Supreme Court justice has lost one.

**The case against.** Courts are supposed to be the branch that can rule against the majority. A judge who must raise money and win a statewide race faces incentives every other candidate faces, and those incentives point toward the interests funding the race. Because judges eventually rule on cases involving their own donors, elected courts create recusal problems that appointed courts do not. Opponents also point to the amendment's silence on partisan versus nonpartisan format: voters were asked to approve a change whose most consequential detail would be filled in later by the Legislature.

The unresolved question sitting underneath both arguments is money. Statewide judicial races in other states have drawn tens of millions of dollars in recent cycles, much of it from out-of-state groups on both sides. Kansas would be adding seven such races to its calendar on a rolling basis. Whether that counts as democratic accountability or as a new pressure on the bench is not a factual dispute — it is a genuine disagreement about what courts are for.

---

## Who lined up where

Backing the amendment: the Kansas Republican Party, the Kansas Chamber, Americans for Prosperity–Kansas, Attorney General Kris Kobach, and former Governor Jeff Colyer.

Opposing it: Governor Laura Kelly, a term-limited Democrat; former Republican Governor Bill Graves and former Democratic Governor Kathleen Sebelius; several former Kansas Supreme Court justices, including a former chief justice who publicly urged a no vote; the Kansas Bar Association; the Kansas Association of School Boards; the ACLU of Kansas; and Kansas Appleseed.

The bipartisan character of the opposition — and the near-total party-line character of the legislative support — is itself part of the story either side tells about the measure.

---

## What happens next

Election-night tallies in Kansas are unofficial. County boards canvass results in the days following the election, and the state canvass certifies the final figures later in the month. Official totals for Amendment 1 come out of that process.

**If it is approved**, the commission is abolished and Kansas moves to elected justices, with the first races in November 2028. The Legislature would then need to pass implementing law — most importantly, deciding partisan versus nonpartisan ballots, and setting rules for judicial campaign finance and recusal.

**If it is rejected**, nothing changes. The commission continues, the governor keeps appointing from three names, retention elections continue on the existing schedule, and Kansas remains the only state where the bar holds a majority on the body that picks the finalists.

---

## The larger question

The Kansas vote is a local decision with a national subtext. Every state has to answer the same question somehow: courts need enough independence to rule against popular majorities, and enough legitimacy that the public accepts those rulings. Appointment systems buy independence and risk looking insular. Elections buy legitimacy and risk turning the bench into another campaign.

There is no arrangement that delivers both without cost. What Kansas voters were asked on Tuesday was not which system is perfect, but which trade-off they would rather live with — and, more bluntly, who they trust to pick the referees.

---

### Quick facts

| | |
|---|---|
| **Vote date** | August 4, 2026 (primary ballot) |
| **Current system** | Nominating commission → governor appoints from 3 names → retention elections |
| **Commission makeup** | 5 attorneys elected by the bar, 4 non-attorneys appointed by the governor |
| **Proposed system** | Direct statewide election, 6-year terms |
| **First elections if approved** | Positions 1–3 in 2028; 4–5 in 2030; 6–7 in 2032 |
| **Legislative vote** | Senate 27–13, House 84–40 — the exact two-thirds minimum in both chambers |
| **National context** | ~21 states already elect justices; Kansas would be the 22nd |

*This article is a general explainer on state judicial selection and does not offer legal advice or endorse a position on the measure. For certified vote totals and official ballot language, consult the Kansas Secretary of State.*
